utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that there was a preliminary matter you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. We are in a situation where we will need some help from our colleagues from Belgrade to help us with leading our witnesses. And since Mr. Petrusic is not able to be with us, we would kindly ask Your Honours to replace Mr. Petrusic with Sasa Lukic. Who would -- we need him I know for sure the next week to lead one or two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you talk about Mr. Sasa Lukic as if he is known to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is on our team from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He work on Beara Defence team and he is our legal assistant, a lawyer from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you need more details, we can provide you in writing if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find out whether we need more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the name is well known but there may be a difference in experience with him in this -- among the Judges in this Chamber. And perhaps we could share what we know and ask ourselves what we still need to know in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else. Then could the witness be brought in. Mr. Traldi, if I understand well you've got one hour and six minutes left from the time estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For everyone's planning purposes, I expect to be about half of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puhalic. Mr. Puhalic, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. May I -- before we continue, may I explain something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it's relevant for us, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since the Prosecutor asked me the other day about some buses that were arriving from the area of Hambarine, Tukovi, Ravcani [phoen], et cetera, I was not -- how do I put this? I wasn't really understanding things right at that moment and then I remembered why I was not at the Trnopolje camp. Then, on the 19th of July, my brother was killed up there in that area, and I was not present for about four or five days at the Trnopolje camp, so I could not remember these buses that were coming in. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to start this morning, sir, with the issue of the video that Mr. Lukic showed you last week. And you'd claimed that the journalists we saw were inside barbed wire, not the prisoners. Now, if the journalists were inside the barbed wire, we would only see barbed wire on one side of the prisoners, right, just between the journalists and them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely. That is what is claimed, that the journalists were within this encircled compound because this wire was around the shop. It wasn't around the camp. It was precisely around that shop. There was this shop there. This shop --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- selling agricultural tools and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand. You've given that explanation on direct, and I'm going to try to be very brief about this topic because you testified that you don't recall whether you were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart now to pull up P206, a longer version of that visit. And show, without playing anything, just 8 minutes, 23.9 seconds, to start us off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we're looking at Trnopolje from just a couple of metres away from the intersection of the two roads that we discussed Thursday that border the camp in this shot; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you agree that we're looking at it from right near the intersection of those roads?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you can see in the foreground, slightly blurry, a man in an olive-drab uniform and then a post between him and the prisoners. And then along the road in the back right of the screen we also see a number of posts; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to go forwards to 9 minutes and 13 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should first state the time-frame the still was taken from. It was 8:23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi announced 8:23. I think it was on the record already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could we go back -- could we go back. Mr. Traldi, you said there was one post there. Apparently the witness confirmed what you'd said you saw. Could we see exactly what the first post -- and perhaps you could assist the usher in using the -- I see the person, but the first post is -- could you ask the usher to or Registry to use the -- how do you call it? The --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the post I indicated in the foreground is just to the right of the man in the olive-drab uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is that one which is now -- that looks kind of like an iron bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the ones, that's what I'm more -- the first one I had no difficulties in --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then if we go to the right side of the picture - the Registry has found them - we see a number of posts along the road ringing the camp on the other side. And, Your Honour, I was using this shot for orientation but I think the point will be a little clearer if we go to the next bit of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say from orientation, you said there was -- where the roads -- let me just get back to the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The intersection, from what direction is the intersection filmed here? At least what is your understanding of from where it is filmed? Is it from south, from north, east? I mean, intersection has a lot of -- or if you say it will become more clear with the stills still to be looked at, then I'll wait. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would say that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I leave it there for the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we move to 9 minutes, 13 seconds. And play -- we won't -- we won't need any audio for this part. Just play from 9 minutes, 13 seconds, to 9 minutes, 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what we clearly saw in that shot is that there is barbed wire both between the camera and the men and between the men and the road that's on the right of the image; right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right-hand side this is some kind of mesh, meshed wire. So it's like -- what? 1 metre, 10, 20 centimetres. That's its height. Regular mesh. There was no barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand you're concerned about the term "barbed." You'd certainly agree that those men are enclosed both in front of them and in what is to their right in the image; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. People were not enclosed, detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, we see wire on multiple sides of these men. Do you recall ever being at the camp when there was wire around them like that, or is this something you don't recall seeing yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In camp? No. I was there. The men who were shown a few moments ago within the compound of that shop, there was this passageway. And then behind the first post, there were these two other posts. How do I explain this to you? There was some kind of gate there and people normally just went through there and looked for the shade. It was very hot. So people would try to seek shelter in the shade from the sun. So it's not that anybody brought them there by force or anything like that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in front -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry to interrupt. I'd asked you a very specific question, which was: Do you recall ever being at the camp yourself and seeing wire around this group of men on multiple sides or is that something that you weren't able to see while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able to see any such thing while I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness explain what the gate then means in this context. You said there was a gate. The gate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It was sort of a passageway, open -- you could see those two posts. Now, who was showing this? And you see there that there is not a proper gate there. There is no door. That meant that people could pass there freely. It was very hot and people were looking for the shade, and then there was this prefabricated building there, and they probably tried to be in the shade there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now if I understand you well, if a gate is an opening, it means that where there is no gate, that there at least there is some kind of closure. I'm not saying whether it is barbed wire or anything else. But a gate means that you can pass there, whereas where there is no gate you can't pass. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course, yes. It was of an open type. Of course one could pass through there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are emphasizing where you could pass, whereas I put to you that if there are certain spots where you can pass, that on other places you may not be able to pass -- at least, there is some kind of a fence of whatever type. Would you agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As can be seen from what has been shown here, there was a fence. But as far as I can remember, even through this fence, this mesh that was underneath the barbed wire, people had again made some kind of passageway. Was it one or two? Again, so that they could pass from that side to this side where the shop was because there was shade there, so they were looking for shade either underneath the tree or in that shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the transcript, page 8, line 12, I hope I said: "Whereas there is no gate, you cannot pass." But that is my recollection of what I said. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm done with this topic. And I have, for the moment, a very specific question about a group called the Manijakosi who you referred to in your statement. Now, that group was formed by Milenko Slijepcevic out of men from his battalion of the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention a group called the Manijakosi in your statement, and what I'm asking you is: Were you aware that that was a group formed by Milenko Slijepcevic out of men from his battalion of the 43rd Brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot tell you because I don't know who it was that had formed that. I just know that that is what their name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm going to focus on your duties now. First, you were the only Slavko Puhalic at Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Puhalic? Yes. But there were other names. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And your evidence is that you were involved in procuring food for Trnopolje. One way food for the camp was procured was via the logistics base at Cirkin Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logistics base and on orders from Major Kuruzovic and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the chief of that logistics base was Mirko Mudrinic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 07140, not to be broadcast but can be addressed in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from the Cirkin Polje logistics base dated the 17th of June, 1992. Here on the first page it's discussing motor vehicles have been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we please have page 4 in both languages. I'm sorry. I'm not sure we have page 4 in the English. My notes, I'm afraid, were in error. If we could have page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this mentions just below point 41 that Cirkin Polje logistics base is being used for distribution of food for the police in the centre, in Prijedor II, army units in Prijedor II, Autotransport, the hospital, Trnopolje, Keraterm, and other purposes. So this confirms what we just discussed, that this was the logistics base -- that this logistics base, rather, was one of the places Trnopolje would get food from; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now if we could have page 7 in the B/C/S and page 13 in the English. Sorry, page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see here an addendum to the report, and it begins: "On the 15th of June, 1992, a number of members of the Territorial Defence Staff of the Serbian army and members of the Cirkin Polje Logistics Base, permanently involved in the securing of Trnopolje," which it describes as a refugees' centre, "addressed themselves to the leadership (command) of the Logistics Base, underscoring the problem of fuel shortage due to which they are not able to carry out security tasks in Trnopolje." And then it refers to a number of such people. Do you see your name at point 3?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it describes you as having taken a Mercedes. It says you're engaged in Trnopolje and working for the military police. Now, does that refresh your recollection as to whether as of the 15th of June you were still engaged at Trnopolje and able to address yourself to this Cirkin Polje logistics base in regards to a vehicle that you'd taken from another man?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. And what's written here --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You've gone a little bit beyond the question. I'm going to ask you a couple of specific follow-up questions regarding your answer. First, you said it was the 9th or the 10th of August when you were taking the cars. Is it your evidence now that you were still at Trnopolje on the 9th or the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say August. I said June. 8th of June. Maybe the 8th or maybe the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this was a green Mercedes; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 300D.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it was in August that it was signed over to you by a contract; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I think it was still on the list of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 7140 receives number P7129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7129 is admitted, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that - in fact on Thursday - that you had a room in what had used to be the Dom building, and you agreed with me that you would speak to prisoners there. In fact, you also conducted interrogations in that room; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were two rooms. One was there in the Dom. I don't know what I would call it. It's a room you could sleep in. And between the Dom and the health centre or medical centre - what shall I call it? - there was another little room where I spoke a couple of times with some locals who were said to have guns in their houses. And I needed to talk to them to prevent some kind of situation that would involve revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You interrogated those men; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was just talk. I couldn't interrogate anyone because I had no - how shall I put it? - orders or something to interrogate people. I wasn't a military policeman as they claim here. I just had a white belt that a friend gave me because I had no other belt to put on. Maybe somebody thought because of that white belt that I was a military policeman, but I wasn't. I was just a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So just to make sure I understand your evidence, your evidence is that Mr. Mudrinic, who you testified knew you, was incorrect that you were a military policeman. And when you spoke to Muslims who were said to have guns in their houses, you were just having a casual conversation with them to avoid the possibility of revenge rather than conducting the questioning that would have been standard at that time. Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you -- as you testified on Thursday, you had the most contact with Major Kuruzovic. You were a link between him and the other men. This would have made you recognisable figure in the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're aware from your Karadzic testimony, aren't you, that people at Trnopolje - including Mr. Gutic, the Serb we discussed who assisted at the medical clinic - have testified here under oath at the Tribunal, though in different cases, that you, in fact, did in that room take part in interrogations where people were beaten; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which Serb you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look briefly at 65 ter 32011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, Mr. Traldi, when you earlier put to the witness what was said in the report, you said he was a military policeman, whereas the report says that he works for the military police which may not be exactly the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is part of Mr. Gutic's testimony in the Tadic case, his sworn testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic's counsel, Mr. Kay, asked: "Mr. Gutic, did Slavko Puhalic have an office in that building?" And Mr. Gutic responded: "As I have said, Slavko Puhalic and the major were spending a large part of their time in those offices while in the camp, but Slavko Puhalic also had an office which was in another building beyond this large building, the former office of the local commune. There were some small offices and that is where Slavko also took inmates for interrogation when they interrogated, when he interrogated them and where some were beaten." That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He's asked about people being called out of Trnopolje. And he says: "Yes, that happened on numerous occasions. I saw twice or more a police vehicle, a van, with a policeman who would come to the camp with such a list, and the deputy commander would come, Slavko Puhalic. He would give him the paper. They would comment on it. They were looking at them. Then Slavko would give that list to the Shift Commander and then he together with the soldiers, with the guards, would go to the camp and was looking for people from those lists, and when they were found they would be taken into the van and driven off." Now, you also took part in taking people out of Trnopolje camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I took part in taking people away. But there was one list or maybe two lists that the police used to come with, and the people who were on those lists - I don't know why, because they were members of some political party or some military formation - I had to pick them up. I couldn't disobey. There were orders. If somebody was wanted, I didn't know why they were wanted, but I would take them and tell them that they needed to go for an interview. What happened later, I don't know. But, yes, in one or two cases -- maybe two or three or four cases, I was involved when the police came. And once even the military police came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can we have 65 ter 32007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up, I would like to ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Involved in what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, I had to execute because Major Kuruzovic told me to join them, to help those people. I asked around if those people were there, and if they were there they should report. And if they were not there, then the police went away without picking anyone up. In two or three cases, I was present with that happened. When I said "involved," I meant I knew about these things that were going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And then you explained: "I had to execute." What did you have to execute? The order you have received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, because the major wasn't there, he told me to be there, to be present, and see when that person was being taken out. I don't remember if there was some laissez-passer and perhaps those people had been registered by the ICRC at that time, so we had to know the precise numbers and register anyone who was taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an excerpt from the Tadic case testimony of Mustafa Mujkanovic who was detained at Trnopolje, and here on the first page at the bottom he is asked if he was beaten at Trnopolje. He says: "Yes, several times."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then turning to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He's asked where, and he says in a building next to the centre called "Laboratory." Now, that's the room you mentioned where you would sometimes speak to people who were thought to have guns in their houses; right?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember whether it was the Laboratory or which other part of the building. I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, beginning at the bottom of the page, he's asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He's asked if he recognised any of the people who took part in the beating. He says: "Slavko from Prijedor, a captain by rank..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then if we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "I saw the insignia, three stars, that is a captain -- and he interrogated me. I do not know, he was a butcher in Prijedor. I believe his family name was 'Puhovski' or something like that ..." Now while he hasn't remembered your family name perfectly, he's clearly talking about you; right?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No, it's not about me. I was not a captain. There was another Slavko. I don't know his last name, but he was a captain. I cannot accept this at all. I cannot accept what he's accusing me of. He is and isn't accusing me. He doesn't name my name correctly and I have never held any rank. I was a regular soldier. I'm not saying such things didn't happen. But whenever these few cases happened in the early days, like beatings or blows or injuries in a couple of cases that I know, I always called the doctor - what's his name? - Idriz. Every morning he would ask me what to do with a certain patient. I don't know if anybody from the outside came in the afternoon when we were gone already or beat somebody up or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: -- stabbed them with a knife. I don't know if such things happened and they failed to report them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- I'm going to stop you there. You were the only Slavko at Trnopolje that was a butcher from Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I was Slavko and I was a butcher. But if there were any other butchers among the guards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now turning to page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- you don't know whether there were any other butchers. Would you know of any butcher in Prijedor by the name Slavko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember all the last names exactly now, but in my trade, I believe there were three or four men called Slavko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you don't remember any of the family names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had some more time to think about it, I think I would remember. But it was a long time ago and it's been a long time since I am not working anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see them when you were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't remember because I most often passed by by car and passed by the place where Major Kuruzovic was. I didn't spend much time going around and meeting other guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never saw any of them near to where the building was as described by Mr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, while I was there, in the morning hours, the time it took to take care of supplies, I don't know. I don't know if somebody came in the afternoon, but I only saw the captain who was there at the entrance, this Slavko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The captain at the entrance? You said that was a Slavko. Was he a butcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to be very efficient, sir. At page 4 of this document, Mr. Mujkanovic describes the beating. He says he was beaten with a baseball bat, cables, boots, hands, even a chair. And on page 6 he confirms that he lost consciousness from this beating and another severe beating he received. Now, what he testified here is the truth, isn't it? He was beaten unconscious in your presence at Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've testified in the Karadzic case and this case, though it was not in your statement in either case, that you were absent from Trnopolje camp for long periods of time during the summer of 1992, that you don't remember what dates precisely you returned, what date you left again. So what I'd put to you is you are doing so because you're aware not just that there are allegations but that there were serious crimes committed in your presence with your involvement at Trnopolje camp in the summer of 1992 and that you were deeply involved in the camp's operations and the interrogations of the prisoners held there. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I have a comment. I didn't do any of those things that you are claiming, nor do I have any involvement in these cases. I don't know. Maybe I offended someone sometime with a bad word or called them a bad name. Maybe I even pushed a person if they called me a bad name such as Chetnik. But as for involvement in killings or rapes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination. I note we are close to the time for the break. I do have one very brief matter to put on the record and perhaps I could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that without the witness. Witness, in your last answer you said: What they say about me about killings and rapes is not true. But most of what was put to you was about interrogations and beatings, not killing and rapes. How about beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said perhaps sometimes in conversation somebody called me a bad name, a derogatory name such as Chetnik, but I was a soldier of the Yugoslav People's Army and later it became the TO or something like that. And as I was saying, maybe I cursed somebody or called them a bad name. Sometimes perhaps I even pushed somebody. But as for involvement in major beatings -- maybe there were such cases and I know about them and they were reported to Kuruzovic. And I reacted every time this Dr. Idriz Merdzanic or whatever was his name, when I came into the room in the morning he would tell me whenever somebody had been injured or stabbed by somebody who had come to that place from the outside, he would ask me what to do. So I cannot claim that such things didn't happen. They happened. But who was involved, I don't know. As for those people who were beaten up, I did go to see them and I asked what had happened, and they would tell me that somebody would come in a military uniform or a police uniform or maybe even wearing a tracksuit. Those people must have been allowed to come in by the guards. But it was not a camp. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you pushed someone, could it have caused any injuries to that person as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't think so or it didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. It would be "no" rather than "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Mr. Traldi, the matter you would like to put on the record is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, two very quick ones. First to ask for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First to ask for a redaction, temporary transcript page 11, line 16 through 25. And the short explanation is that's the reason I was asking the document not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the second is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- redaction, Madam Registrar, can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the second, Mr. President, is I've been informed that my notes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've been informed that my notes were inaccurate as to the ethnicity of Mr. Gutic and I apologise to the Chamber, but we won't, of course, rely on my suggestion that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll not rely on that. Did you intend to make the ethnicity of that person a relevant issue anyhow? Because then we should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I didn't. And I didn't inquire -- I didn't ask the witness to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But I had misspoken on the record and wanted to correct it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you not know whether he is a Serb or is he in your view not a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm told, though I've been on my feet and haven't confirmed it myself, is that he is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break and will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber assumed that you would still have some questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Chamber assumed correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the last document my learned friend discussed with this witness. It's 65 ter 32007. We'll need from the line 23 on this page. This gentleman, Mustafa Mujkanovic, describes two beatings. And can we have the next page, please. In line 7 we can see the name of the man who took him for interrogation. It's Mladen Mitrovic. And then we need the bottom of the page, line 23 and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then he was asked -- I quote, 23: "Q. When you were taken to the lab and beaten, did you recognise any of the people who took part in that beating?" Answer, in line 25: "Yes, one Slavko from Prijedor, a Captain by rank -- I mean, I saw the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "... insignia, three stars ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then my learned friend read the rest of this paragraph until line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you told us that you're not a captain. Did you wear three stars on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then this man, in line 7 -- I'm going to read this out to you again to see what it was that he said. [In English] Question, I quote: "Sir, the uniforms that these men wore, did the uniforms have any kind of insignia on them?"

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, just a moment, please. Before I read further, this is what I'm going to ask you: What kind of insignia did you have on your uniform? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I didn't have any insignia on the uniform except for what I said, the white belt that was given to me by some military policeman. I cannot tell you exactly who it is because he went to the military police and then I was supposed to take a man, I think his name was Saban, that's what he they called him, I don't know his exact last name. No, no, not Saban. That was his brother. It was -- well, I was there at the military command and I left from there, and they asked me to take this man up there to Trnopolje. Of course I accepted, and I asked if they had a belt, perhaps, and they said, "Well, we have a white one if you want," and I took that. So the only thing I had by way of insignia was a white belt, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll stop reading the transcript for a moment now and I'll ask you this: Did you belong to the military police?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the unit that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Well, I belonged to the 43rd -- now, was it the TO -- whatever. I don't know how to put this. The 43rd Motorised Brigade of Prijedor. Since I had come from Croatia as a JNA soldier and then I joined that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you have -- actually, what was it that Major Kuruzovic headed at the time when you were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he headed the TO or that Crisis Staff or -- I don't know. I cannot tell you exactly what he was at the time. At any rate, it's something like that probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were in Trnopolje, did you belong to that unit that was headed by Major Kuruzovic, or that establishment, if you will?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you wear a kokarda?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No. Otherwise, my family had this - what do I call it? - Yugoslav partisan spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. In this answer in line 9 and further on, when this man was asked whether these men who beat him had any insignia, now he says, and I quote: [In English] "Yes, yes, there were, there were. There were kokardas also on their caps or on those caps. They are round caps...," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have now page 4 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you, first of all, what kind of an accent do you have?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Ijekavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read this out to you what this witness says, from line 1 onwards. [In English] And I quote: "The people that were in the room, this first time that you were beaten, did any of the people in that room use a non-local dialect when they spoke? "A. Yes. "Q. What was did dialect or accent that you recognised? "A. From Serbia and Montenegro. They were people who came up from outside most probably." [Interpretation] So for the record just this: Do you speak using the same accent that people from Serbia use?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we need page 2 of this document, line 2 -- Page 5, sorry, line 2. Now we are on a second beating this man described. We are finished with the first one. And for the second one, on lines 13 and 15 of this page, he mentions the names of the people who took part in that second beating. It's Mitrovic and Goran Nisevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the question put to that person, there is no reference to beating but that the witness was taken by this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are right, Your Honour. I -- there was nobody actually then mentioned for the second beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know who Mitrovic is and who Goran Nisevic is?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I cannot remember. They were probably guards or somebody who had come from the outside or perhaps they are some neighbours from there. I don't know. There were quite a few people who were neighbours who came there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've mentioned neighbours, was there a danger of revenge?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes. As a matter of fact, if I may, I can tell you about a specific case. One morning I came and a lady went out and said that her husband was missing for two or three days or so. And then I informed Major Kuruzovic about that, and then he ordered me to stay there, spend the night there at that collection centre. I accepted that. I spent the night at Dom with this Albanian man. There was this small room there, and I made some kind of a bed there and I would spend two or three nights there. While I spent those nights there, nothing of significance happened, no one was taken out, or this or that did not happen. There was a girl, rather, that day she asked to see me and she said what her name was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Does that have anything to do with revenge? I mean, the story that you keep telling us?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm just telling you that nothing really happened. Somebody came, took that man out, and I think that even the guard who was there, there with Major Kuruzovic, confirmed -- I don't know whether he confirmed who he was or -- well, maybe. Maybe. Precisely for those reasons. Kuruzovic probably -- well, maybe some of the neighbours got that man out and this man never came back. It may be this kind of revenge or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you say got him out. So you keep taking me back all the time. On transcript page 31677 - our transcript, that is - I'm going to read out the question and your answer, and then I'm going to ask another question. I quote: [In English] "Q. And you were aware that detainees were killed in Trnopolje camp; right? "A. Well, was it one or two cases. That's something that I heard." [Interpretation] Were there any killings within the compound of the collection centre of Trnopolje, and what did you hear? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: As far as I know, not a single killing was committed. I know of one case, probably it was an elderly man and he died a natural death, and then the doctor asked what he was supposed to do. And then I said that the man should be driven out and buried at a particular place, and that was done. They drove him -- well, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's a natural death.

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you say you heard of one or two cases. What is that?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: As far as I know, in two cases there were two killings, as far as I can remember. One was when people went somewhere outside the camp. Now, did they go home, and a soldier went with them, and then while they were at home they probably wandered off. And what were they looking for? Money, jewelry, whatever. A patrol came along and these people were killed. And then when this young man came back, he said what it was that had happened. And then I went to Major Kuruzovic -- actually, it was the following day. And then I went to the major and informed him. Immediately after that, after receiving this information, we got into the car and we went to Kozarac up there so that he would see with the police what it was that had happened. So that is this one case. The other case, I don't know. Was he -- actually, did he give a pass to two men to help some man do something. And now whether this man killed these people after that? As far as I know, this case was even prosecuted. I cannot be sure whether there was a trial or not, but I know that he did report that. So all of that happened outside the compound of the Trnopolje centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Document P7126 was shown to you. This document contains a title, namely: "Results of the 1993 census in Prijedor municipality (local communes)." This is what I'm interested in. P3791, that's the number. This is a report from Kozarski Vjesnik. This is what I'd be interested in: Do you know whether there was a census in the municipality of Prijedor during the war in 1993?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I think that a census took place every ten years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what's the typo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me? Typo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there is a typo in this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Title. I'm sorry. I misunderstood that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be well on the record, but I was relying on what I heard rather than on what I did read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have on our screens 65 ter number 07157, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report on the work of a logistics base. The date is September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the last page, please. [In English] Sorry. It's a longer document. Actually, I need page 2 in both versions. I'm sorry. Because it's the end of this document, since there are some additional documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know Mirko Mudrinic, you've heard about him?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what jurisdiction, what authority, Major Kuruzovic had over this base?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I don't know. I think the Crisis Staff was there. Now, what his jurisdiction was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the Cirkin Polje logistics base?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the connection was between the logistics base and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the logistics base operated in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say with any certainty because I don't know when it operated. At that time, I was already on the front line. It was probably operative at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have P3708, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we see that document on the screen, a document from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, 9 July 1992, did you receive reports about the possibility of attack by Muslim forces on the collection centre of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuruzovic talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here in paragraph 4 - it could be the fifth paragraph but it's linked with the fourth - a group of extremists --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not found this text yet. Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph under item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "A group of 30-40 extremists from the village of Kozarac, near Prijedor, plan to attack the prison camp in the village of Trnopolje ..." Do you know if there were still remaining armed groups in the villages around Kozarac in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes, I know that the army pursued them, constantly chased them. I don't know how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P3891.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an overview of the conclusions adopted by the Executive Council of Prijedor municipality. In fact, we have a summary of conclusions towards the bottom of the page, conclusions, orders, and decisions by the Crisis Staff, War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we need page 3 in both versions. Third paragraph from below in English, and the third from the top in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Conclusion number," such and such, "of 2nd July 1992, forbidding the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm. Signed Crisis Staff, War Presidency." While working in Trnopolje, did you know who was allowed to let people out of Trnopolje? Who decided these things?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: The only one who had the authority to release someone was Major Kuruzovic. Without his permission, nobody was allowed out. Nobody could leave the centre, go back home, or go to the centre of Prijedor or Banja Luka. Nobody could do that without his permission, because there were check-points to pass and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know from whom he received such orders or permissions?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I don't know. It could have been the Crisis Staff, the police, or the army. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhalic. That's all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I ask Mr. Traldi whether he has any further questions for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you explained that a white belt was given to you by people from the military police. I think you said: Well, they asked me whether I would take one, and then you accepted that. Could you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No. I mean, I don't know which military policemen were there when I returned to take that gentleman to Trnopolje. And my trousers were a bit too large, they were kind of falling off, and I asked, "Do you maybe have a belt I could use," and they gave me that white belt. I believe it had the buckle of the military police on it. So I accepted it from them. I thanked them and left. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the person, you didn't know that specific military policeman?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe he was -- I believe his name was Stevica Sredic. He's actually a friend of mine who had been with me in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the reason why I'm asking you, because you said: Well, just a military policeman. But at the same time you call him a friend. So therefore, I'm -- because that's one of the answers you gave earlier - I'm referring to page 13 of the transcript - you said: "I just had a white belt that a friend gave me because I had no other belt to put on." So I was puzzled by the fact that on the one hand you say a military policeman and on the other hand you say it was a friend. Was it a friend, was it no friend?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I asked you this question a minute ago, I said could you tell us who that was, the person that gave you the belt. I read to you what your answer was. "No. I mean, I don't know which military policemen were there when I returned to take that gentleman to Trnopolje. And my trousers were a bit too large, they were kind of falling off, and I asked, 'Do you maybe have a belt I could use,' and they gave me that white belt. I believe it had the buckle of the military police on it. So I accepted it from them. I thanked them and left. That's all." And then I asked you again: "But the person, you didn't know that specific military policeman?" Then you said: "I don't know. I believe his name was Stevica Sredic. He's actually a friend of mine who had been with me in Croatia." That is a change in your answer within a minute from not knowing to being a friend. Do you have an explanation for that sudden change in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: As I was explaining that, I was trying to cast my mind back to remember who that person was. When you asked me who the person was who had given me the belt, I tried to remember because there were several people there. And now I think - in fact I'm sure - that he is the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move to another subject. Do you know Mr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Gutic?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Gutic? No. I think the gentleman was a technician in that service for assistance, the auxiliary service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any specific reason for these persons why they would mention your name or refer to you in any other way and lying about your involvement in beatings?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I explained to you that I am not the person that they are pointing to. I don't know any other reason. This Gutic man, I believe he was with that Dr. Merdzanic. I don't know if he too was a doctor or a helper. In any case, I saw them together. And I don't know Mr. Mujkanovic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you say: "... I explained to you that I am not the person that they are pointing to." Now, we've heard your answers in relation to Mr. Mujkanovic, but for the other person there seems to be no great doubt that he's referring to you, is there?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe he's talking about me but I don't know for what reason why. Maybe I was unable to help somebody when they asked. Maybe that's his way of getting back at me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I leave it to that. One final question: What is the dialect which is usually spoken by those who grow up in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: What do you mean by, "I was involved when the police came"?
utterances.text: Ijekavian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that spoken in Serbia proper as well or is it not? If you know. If you don't know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The previous answer was "Ijekavian." And the witness's answer now is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe in Serbia Ekavian is spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this may as a matter of fact resolve some misunderstanding. Yes, for that reason, page 26, line 6, perhaps, should also be looked at in the English. Mr. Traldi, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Puhalic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions, questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I hope I was able to assist to the extent of my abilities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll start reading a decision, a decision which is delivered. It is a decision by the Chamber on the admission of documents used and tendered through the testimony of Vladimir Lukic on 8 through 10 September 2014. Five documents tendered by the Prosecution were marked for identification during the cross-examination of Witness Lukic. These are P6730, P6733, P6734, P6740, and P6742. On the 18th of December, 2014, the Prosecution indicated via e-mail that it no longer sought the admission of P6730. This document will therefore be marked not admitted. P6733 was marked for identification pending a B/C/S translation. A translation has now been uploaded into e-court, and under document ID 0000-5130a-BCST. The e-mail was -- an e-mail in this respect was sent on the 8th of January of this year. And Madam Registrar is instructed to attach the translation to P6733, and the Chamber admits P6733 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the remainder of the P numbers later. Good morning - yes, it's still morning - Mr. Radinkovic, I take it. Mr. Radinkovic, before you give evidence the Rules require that you give the solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radinkovic. Please be seated. Mr. Radinkovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with our procedure here, would you please tell us slowly your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Radomir Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, did you at one point in time give a written statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we call up in e-court 65 ter 1D0295a [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record, the number is 1D02395a. Could we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, it's now in front of you. For the record, would you tell the Court if you recognise the signature on the last page? Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise it. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And another question: The date, 8 December 2013, is it written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Today when you gave the solemn declaration in this courtroom, undertaking to tell the truth, and after reviewing what is written here, do you still stand by this statement as truthful and given to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by it. It is truthful and given to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you again, would you answer the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender the statement of Radomir Radinkovic, 65 ter 1D02395a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one observation, if I may, Your Honour. Below paragraph number 40, there is reference to a document bearing the number P3724, and that's a Karadzic -- a P number from the Karadzic Prosecution, and in this case that document has the P number 2908.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2395a receives number D900, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The statement of -- D900 is admitted into evidence. Perhaps one question, Mr. Stojanovic. Often the format of statements taken by the Defence is such that we know who took the statement, when the statement was taken, who were present. That is different here. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have been mistaken, Mr. Stojanovic. One second. Yes, you asked about the statement taken by the Karadzic Defence. Still, dates, persons present, and who took the statement is still sometimes interesting information, but I accept that this is at least not common when you take statements from the Karadzic Defence and adopt them in the Mladic case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At this point in time, I would like to ask that I be allowed to tender a table that has to do with matching adjudicated facts as you had suggested to us in previous situations that were similar. It's 65 ter number 1D05332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any -- I have -- is it on the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the table of concordance as to adjudicated facts identified in the witness statement. Yes. And that is now -- the number is 1D02395a. Please proceed. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was confused by the fact that what we have on our screen now is a table of concordance which is not exactly the same as the one I looked at before I came to court. I looked at the one which was attached to the 92 ter motion. But it's clear now that the table of concordance, as we see it now on our screen, accurately refers to 1D02395a. No further objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just again another observation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In this table of concordance there is for some reason the text of an adjudicated fact, and with respect to facts 465, 473, and 484, the rendering of the adjudicated fact is -- is not entirely accurate. So while we can consider, of course, what the witness says about the fact to be significant, just a note of caution: We can't rely on this rendering of the adjudicated fact in this table of concordance, but all the other numbering is perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any reason why the text of the adjudicated fact does not fully reflect what the Chamber admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we used a text that is derived from the adjudicated facts as stated in our decision. If there is any difference, we will certainly check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is it that you referred to the Karadzic adjudicated facts rather than to the Mladic adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That statement is from the Karadzic case as well, and it is an integral part of the statement that is before us and that has been admitted into evidence in this case and that we are tendering for admission into evidence in this case. And it includes paragraphs 8, 9, 10, 11, and 13 of the statement of the witness we have today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This all happens if statements are copied from other cases. Let's move on. I do not understand the observations to be an objection. Madam Registrar, the table of concordance would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5332 receives number D901, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D901 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just for my understanding, Mr. Stojanovic, ask: In this column "Text of Adjudicated Fact," are these the adjudicated facts literally quoted from our case in Mladic or from the Karadzic case? Because in the heading of that column it's unclear if it relates to Mladic or Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand our Case Manager, Your Honour, these are adjudicated facts -- or, rather, this is the text of adjudicated facts from our case, the Mladic case, and they fully correspond to adjudicated facts in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm afraid that this is wrong. The adjudicated fact in the Mladic case number 473 reads: "Detainees at the Manjaca camp witnessed beatings being inflicted on other detainees." And if you look in your -- on the list we just have admitted into evidence, we see the text in the column "Text of Adjudicated Fact" is different from that one. I just want to make you aware of this fact that it seems to be that these facts are taken from the Karadzic case and not from the Mladic case. I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it's your responsibility if you rely on your Case Manager, that you verify and you're responsible for the accuracy of what you're telling us. And I would urge you to be more --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- serious in that respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. And we are going to check whether there are any differences involved. With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to tender two other documents accompanying this statement: 1D -- actually, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number seems to be 65 ter 07038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the number you wanted to refer to, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. 07038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 7038 receives number D902, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D902 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the time has come to take the break. And after the break, I would like to read out the witness's summary, and then I'd like to put a few questions to the witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you announced that you would tender two more documents. I think we've heard of one. Is that -- Mr. Stojanovic, do you have another one or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. Since this other document already has a P number, so there will be no need for me to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd like to tender only one document, and you said two. But that's hereby corrected. We'll take the break. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes and we'd like to see you back after that, and then we'll not limit ourselves to administrative matters. Although, attesting to a statement is not really an administrative matter, but then we'll go further to the substance of your testimony. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask the next witness to be escorted into the courtroom, and I think it can be -- Madam Registrar, it can be -- the witness can be escorted already. It's very short. It is about Witness Ratko Skrbic, who is scheduled to testify next week on the 23rd of February. The Prosecution has indicated that it will not need to cross-examine this witness if no further information is elicited beyond what is contained in the statement. Mr. Lukic, which means that you're invited again to postpone the testimony of that witness. We have to check with you whether you intend to put any additional questions to the witness, because that's the condition under which the Defence -- the Prosecution refrains from cross-examination. And if so, then you should make that part of your discussions with the Registrar. I don't know whether the meeting has been scheduled already or has taken place already, but in order to explore the practical implications of what you suggested and that is to hear those witnesses through videolink rather than to change their status from 92 ter to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Only to add to that I think that at this moment we have three witnesses in Belgrade who could go this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we are waiting for a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on your meeting the practical --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but we didn't have a meeting yet with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but, of course, you'll understand that the Registrar may have his own problems, and finally we'll decide the issue once we have received all the information we would need; that is, practical information included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it's clear that the witness will not be called for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we start, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber was informed that e-court is not functioning well. I don't know whether it will be -- it's not functioning at all. Therefore, I suggest that you start by reading your summary, that if you have any further questions to the witness, that the witness will be provided with the redacted statement, and that as soon as you need to call certain documents which cannot be seen on e-court, that you either have a hard copy which could then be put on the ELMO or that we would have to stop because we can't continue without looking at relevant documents you would like to put to the witness. At the same time, you are also invited to see whether you can arrange your examination-in-chief in such a way that we would not run into trouble easily and that you would perhaps start with those questions for which we do not necessarily need e-court. This caveat is on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I would like to read out the summary of Witness Radomir Radinkovic's statement. Witness Radomir Radinkovic, when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was mobilised as desk officer for security and intelligence affairs in the 1st Krajina Corps, holding the rank of staff sergeant. He carried out different tasks there up until the end of the war; and inter alia, he spent part of his military service in the POW camp at Manjaca practically from the moment when it was established up until when it was disbanded. His task was security assessment of POWs, security support for the camp, and operative work with POWs, reporting to the superior command, and proposing measures of protection. These reports were sent to the superior command at least once a week and, when necessary, every day. In his statement he describes what the camp looked like, the facilities where the POWs were put up, as well as the structure and organisation of the security for prisoners and the role of the civilian police in securing the camp. He speaks in detail about how POWs were treated at the moment when they were taken in, and he speaks about their screening. He says that there was a commission for receiving them that consisted of the camp commander, a doctor, a military policeman, and a security and intelligence organ who identified the persons that were brought in, made them aware of their rights and responsibilities, and afterwards made sure that they were medically examined and put in the right facilities. The witness explains certain incidents that occurred in the Manjaca camp and incidents related to the transportation and bringing in of POWs from Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most at Manjaca. After they were admitted into the camp, they were treated in accordance with the status of prisoners of war according to the Geneva Conventions concerning regulation and verification, regular food supplies, sufficient quantities of drinking water, and medical care, regular visits from the ICRC, and accommodation, which meant beds for the officers who were POWs and the rest slept on straw and had a sufficient number of blankets.
