Finally, he speaks about his own view of the adjudicated facts, investigations, and measures that were taken against persons from the security of the camp who unlawfully carried out their duties as well as their prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have just finished the translation of the summary, so we did not hear the question put by Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters had just finished to interpret your summary when you already put the question to the witness. So would you please put the question to the witness again so that we receive interpretation of that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, I would just like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what this looked like, the internal and external security of the Manjaca facility. What did these two forms of security imply?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Internal security was just the isolated part where the POWs were, and external security pertained to the entire camp; that is to say, barbed wire over 2 metres high, and there was just one gate through which the camp could be entered, and there was barbed wire all around. In addition to this barbed wire, the external one, the hangars where the prisoners were were also surrounded by a different wire, again 2 metres high, and there was this entrance. This was locked all the time. It is only military policemen that could unlock this, when they were bringing people in for interrogations, et cetera. As for this area, no one had access except for the patrol of military policemen who were on duty on that day -- I beg your pardon. As for civilians, it was the International Red Cross and from time to time journalists could enter that area and be with the POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just pause for a second for the interpretation to finish. The next thing I want to ask you, and you did speak about this partly in your statement, civilian police inspectors, did they have an opportunity, and if so, on the basis of which procedure, did they have the opportunity to enter that area and have contact with the POWs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian police could not enter that other area at all, this so-called second security area. They could only reach the offices where we were, we the security organs, where we were interviewing these persons. And they were in this other part, the more open one, the more open part. So it is only there that civilian policemen could come, and then certain prisoners would be brought to them for interviews or interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When somebody was brought for an interview with an inspector of the civilian police, would any of you - the security detail of the facility or anyone from the administration of the facility - participate in the interview or attend the interview?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not, because we were a military structure and they were a civilian structure. They were doing their job. We were responsible for providing a military patrol to bring that person. They would have to report to us about anything they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were receiving a new batch of POWs and when you were carrying out the procedure you described, did you notice any people with visible injuries?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. There were many more cases than we had expected, unfortunately, and that's why we introduced this medical checkup during the admission process, to assess the gravity of injuries, bruises, or whatever. And because a large group was brought from one collection centre, people who were emaciated in a really bad state, we also started making records.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were admitting someone into Manjaca, if you noticed that a person had visible injuries, where would it be recorded? Where would it be noted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: The commission I mentioned would report it to the camp commander, and we would give our proposals in case of serious injuries, and there were really serious injuries, we would make a proposal to transfer these people to the hospital. And since the doctor who was there could not provide adequate medical care, they would be transported to a hospital in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Inside the facility at Manjaca itself, was there some sort of infirmary, some sort of medical facility where such people could be given medical assistance and care?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called it the medical hub. One room where a paramedic was constantly on duty. And among the prisoners, there was always at least one doctor. And, of course, in that infirmary there was medication, antibiotics, medical supplies that could be dispensed to the prisoners. And persons on duty from each pavilion could wake up the policemen on duty and ask for help. There were cases when at 3.00 a.m. in the morning, a person who needed to be transported to the hospital was provided with transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did this commission service operate, the representatives of the prisoners vis-à-vis the administration of the camp?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Each pavilion, each hangar as we called it, had their monitor, and a senior representative who was allowed, who had the right to come to the gate and tell the policemen if they needed something, and then this message would be transmitted to our service and we would decide what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a time when the administration of the camp exerted any influence on the prisoners regarding who they would elect as their representative?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They elected completely on their own the person whom they trusted the most, and they even selected the head of their kitchen, the person who would cook for them, and it was entirely their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about a specific name you mention in your statement, Dr. Eniz Sabanovic. Would you tell the Court, do you know what happened with this doctor? Do you know how long he was at Manjaca, until when?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Until he was exchanged. I can't remember exactly when he was sent out to be exchanged, but he was among the first to arrive at Manjaca and one of the first to be exchanged. From the very first day, we appointed him medical doctor for POWs, and he carried out that duty to our utmost satisfaction and to the satisfaction of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radinkovic, for your answers. That would be all for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Radinkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You find her to your right. Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radinkovic. Maybe you remember me. I cross-examined you two years ago as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I remember you, fondly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I'm going to cross-examine you again today. And I just want to start by clearing up a couple of things from your statement and tying them together, perhaps a little more coherently. Now, when you said in your statement that you testified against -- in the Banja Luka District Court against a group of military policemen who were prosecuted for beating Filipovic and Bender to death, that was in 2006, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the military policemen you were talking about were VRS military policemen; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the security of the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this trial wasn't a military trial?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: The military service did their part of the criminal investigation --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, no --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: -- to establish what they had done in the compound of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, I didn't ask you what the military service did, did I? I asked you: This trial wasn't a military trial, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was a civilian court. The district court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We object to the vagueness of the question. Twice we heard the question "military trial." It creates confusion. What does it mean, "military trial"? Is it a trial against military personnel or trial before a military court? And it would be a military court in that year when the trial was held. That's why I believe that the question phrased in this way, to include words "military court," is vague and could be confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness has answered the question. Apparently it has not confused him, and the question is not such that it's inadmissible for being too vague. Therefore the objection, although post-answer, is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those policemen in whose trial you testified were convicted for the murders and other crimes and those -- that's the group you refer to at paragraph 30 of your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. I also just want to be a little bit clearer on your function in Manjaca. As intelligence and security officer, your job was to interrogate prisoners; right? That's what you did at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the objectives. There were other ones but that was the basic one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your job was to talk to the people who'd been brought in and to find out whether they'd been captured in combat; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, we were supposed, if we didn't have enough information about the captured person, to look for information ourselves, information related to security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So information relating to whatever military unit they might have come from, the name of the unit, the type of the unit, things like that; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: That kind of information, too. But since it was 1992, the very beginning of the war, we were also looking for information about possible preparations for actions against the Army of Republika Srpska that could be ongoing among that population. We were looking for any relevant facts that would be of use to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your professional superior would have been the chief -- or actually, the 1st Krajina Corps' assistant commander for security; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, our superior - the superior to all of us, the team working at Manjaca - was the recipient of our reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was Colonel Bogojevic, who you mention in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Before him there was Lieutenant-Colonel Stevilovic. He was killed and Bogojevic came to replace him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Bogojevic then was a member of the staff of the 1st Krajina Corps, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So he could directly issue orders to you, but he could also pass on orders from his own superiors; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it worked. We were sending our reports to the command and we also received reports from our superior commands; that is to say, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So the reports that you talked about in your statement in paragraphs 14 and 15, they would actually go a couple of places. They would go up your professional chain, through Colonel Bogojevic to General Talic, and they would also go to Colonel Popovic, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: We as professional security organs were not really required to provide all security assessments to the camp commander. We were required to provide them exclusively to our professional security department and Mr. Bogojevic, and we also briefed the camp commander verbally on a regular basis so that he should be aware of some things that might be relevant to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to get you to confirm some things you -- actually, before I get there, I want to ask you one more thing, then. We've heard evidence from other security officers in this case who talk about the professional chain of responsibility within the VRS, and I wonder if you can confirm that, militarily speaking, the security and intelligence officer was the professional organ in charge of the military police? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Military Police Battalion was part of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. It was available for the corps command to use automatically by virtue of their position, and normally all of us security organs went about our job professionally. There were not many variations in the way we worked. We all provided official notes up along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about whether or not you did your job professionally. I wanted -- I asked you about whether, militarily speaking, the military police were professionally subordinate to the security and intelligence organ. That's how it worked in the Bosnian Serb Army, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. One squad from the Military Police Battalion was detached to provide security to the camp. It was directly under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, and this military police was part of the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to talk about the camp in more detail for a few minutes, I want to get you to confirm a little bit of the evidence that you gave in the Karadzic case. You can confirm that the prisoners that came to Manjaca camp were brought to Manjaca camp in June, July, and August 1992 came from Kljuc and Prijedor and Sanski Most, among other places; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that. That's approximately the chronology. They came in separate batches from Kljuc, then from Prijedor or Sanski Most, I don't know the exact sequence. But they came in separate groups, never together.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the camp population numbered in the thousands. At one point in your Karadzic evidence, you said it got up as high as 4.000 or 4.500 detainees. Do you confirm that today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not confirm that then and I cannot confirm it now. At no point had there been more than 2.400 people, considering that the overall number that turned over through the Manjaca camp was 4.400 people. There was no moment when there were 4.500 people there inside together. They couldn't fit in, simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, now that e-court is working, I wonder if we could have a look at Mr. Radinkovic's testimony in the Karadzic case. It was 65 ter number 32013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Indeed, luckily enough, e-court is functioning again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just if I may, Your Honour, so that we all stay bright until the next break, I wonder, completely aside, if we can ask for the temperature to be reduced in the courtroom just by a couple of degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A couple of degrees might make us freeze, but it is relatively warm in the courtroom and we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar had asked for it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter number 32013. I'd like to go to e-court page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently there is still a problem with the e-court. What we could do is to take an earlier break than usual. That would be a break lasting until 25 minutes past 1.00 and then have a last 50 minutes until the adjournment for the day. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I mean, I could read the testimony out, Your Honours, because, you know, it hasn't been translated into B/C/S. That's the nature of transcript. But I know Your Honours prefer to have the witness see it and the hard copy I have -- oh, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently we have something on our screen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we try going to page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Radinkovic, we had this same argument when you testified two years ago. You said originally, when I asked you the question, at line 1, that the maximum at one time was around 2.000 because some people left and new ones came. And then I reminded you about the evidence that you gave in the state court during one of your previous testimonies. At line 6 -- pardon me, at line 7, I reminded you: "... there you said that the population ranged, actually." And that it was almost 3.000. And then further you said at one point it went up to maybe 4- to 4500. And then responded to me and the Judges in the Karadzic trial, you said, and I quote: "That's what I said. It varied. Sometimes there were more, sometimes less." So you told me a couple of minutes ago that the population was never above something in the neighbourhood of 2.000 but you testified two years ago that at one point it went up to 4.000 or 4.500. Are you changing the evidence you gave?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not changing my evidence. I said before the court in Sarajevo that the number varied and there could never have been 4.000 people at one time. And I said here in the Karadzic case that the number varied because people came and went and I stand behind that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what you said to the court in Sarajevo during your testimony in the Kondic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 32015, e-court page 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. We have -- I got a copy two years ago of your evidence in the Kondic case, and here at page 68 you were asked about the prison population. At line 7, you were asked: "Can you make an estimate?" You responded: "Well, maybe 4-, 4.500. This is my rough estimate. I did not receive them my -- of my own or send them to exchange." So you said in the court in Sarajevo 4.500. If it was a small number, maybe we wouldn't be quibbling, but this isn't quibbling. We are talking about a difference of over 2.000 prisoners, Mr. Radinkovic. Are you changing your evidence from what you gave to the court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see that statement in our language. I can see it only in English. But I know very well that I maintained in Sarajevo as well as in the Karadzic case that there could never have been that many people at any one time. I know that there are books, log-books, registering the exact number of prisoners of war at -- on any particular day in the camp. It was not our job to keep these records. Our job was to process them and to organise various activities related to exchange, et cetera, tasks that we received along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a long answer, Witness, but let's try to get to -- what could be and what was registered is one thing. Did you say in the state court, and you say you can't read it, it's not in B/C/S, I again read it slowly to you: "All the records were sent to the command and the command was forwarding them to authorities." And that's -- Ms. Edgerton, I want you to do it yourself. Why is that? Because where the number is mentioned here, it starts apparently on the previous page what the subject matter is. So therefore, for us to know exactly what we are talking about, we should go one page back at least. That's one. Second, where the witness, from what I understood, may challenge whether this is what he said, although he did apparently not or not unambiguously in the Karadzic case, is there any audio recording? Is there -- how is this transcribed? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just by way of information, this is transcribed from an audio recording of the witness's testimony in the Kondic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And is that audio recording available if need be?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then could we go back to the previous page to find out whether these numbers are numbers about persons in Manjaca at one time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll begin -- we'll go back to page 67 of your testimony in the Kondic case. And starting at line 16, the question from the prosecutor was: "Right. You said that there were four stables with prisoners." You responded: "Yes." "And that there were up to 3.000 people in the camp." You responded: "Yes. "How many people in total went through the camp?" You responded: "I don't know. I didn't work alone there. "But according to the records and the statistics?" You responded: "All the records were sent to the Command and the Command was forwarding to other authorities." "So you don't know?" Was the question. You responded: "I don't know." And then you were asked: "Can you make an estimate?" "Well, maybe 4, 4.500. This is my rough estimate. I did not receive them myself ... of my own or send them to exchange." And then it goes on to ask you specific questions about the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- Witness, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second. Ms. Edgerton, what we see on the last line is how many people went through the camp, whereas your focus and what you did put to the witness was very much how many prisoners there were at one point in time. Unless you have other sources to bring this to the attention of the witness or if you have another explanation as why you translate prisoners going through Manjaca camp into prisoners being at one time in Manjaca camp, I think we should be very careful not to mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please go back again to page 67, because I think the relevant question was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the last line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it is the last line and you read it out to the witness, but it didn't go into the transcript of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But it should be in the transcript. So perhaps you read or I could read the last line, which is the introduction to what then follows on the next page is: "How many people in total went through the camp?" Then it's good that we have a correct -- an accurate transcript, but do you have any explanation as to why you translate this into 4- or 4500 people at the same time in the camp which you have put several times to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I -- only to go back to his assertion in the Karadzic case, and completely accepting my misstatement of course, Your Honours, and apologies, and I can apologise to the witness as well. But I do go back to his testimony in the Karadzic case where he did agree to that number. And I will be asking for that page in the Karadzic transcript to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he -- whether he did or not, we'll -- if you put it again -- at least in this transcript, there is no accurate basis for what you put to the witness, and we'll now further look then at Karadzic. And of course there, we have to ask ourselves how it was put to the witness then and what his exact answers are. So I take it that you will bring us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honours. Perhaps we could go back to then 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness can put on his earphones again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go back to 65 ter number 32013, which is the transcript of testimony from the Karadzic case we looked at earlier, e-court page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you would tell us first of all what you intend to read out to the witness so that we already can cast an eye on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps also previous page, because it -- the page starts with -- it therefore reads that number. Then, of course, we would have to know what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see there at the bottom of the page. Perhaps you start -- perhaps you start at line 20. That gives the best introduction to what then follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I get this in Serbian, in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have to carefully listen. There is no B/C/S version of this document. If there is any need to hear it again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- just ask. Madam Prosecutor will slowly read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged a bit, the lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radinkovic, to stay on this topic for a little while more, just to make sure we have your position correctly, I'd like to read to you some portion of your cross-examination in the Karadzic case relating to the number of prisoners. From line 20 in your transcript, I asked you: "First, you can confirm, I take it, that particularly between June and August 1992 Manjaca received a massive number of prisoners; right?" And you said: "Yes, and even the number of these arrivals is stated. "Q. Well -- okay, talking about the number, at its -- its fullest, the prisoner population at Manjaca was in excess of 3.500 people; right?"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go over to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then your answer was: "It never reached that number at any one time. The maximum at one time was around 2.000, because some people left and new ones came. They departed to be exchanged. They were transported to third countries or elsewhere. And some new people came." And then my question was: "Well, now, are you quite sure about those figures? Because I've read your testimony that you gave in 2011 to the state court in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there you said that the population ranged, actually. At page 29, you said it was almost 3.000, and then at page 68 you said at one point it went up to maybe 4-, 4.500?" And then your answer was: "That's what I said. It varied. Sometimes there were more, sometimes less. That's what I was trying to explain."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness take off his earphones again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just reading the full transcript before explaining what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, I earlier referred to misleading the witness by translating "through the camp" into being 4- to 4.500 at one point in time. I noticed that the question in the Karadzic case was as misleading as I considered the question you put to the witness today. And then the answer of the witness is not unambiguous, because he said: "That's what I said. It varied." Now, in your question you are talking about almost 3.000 and at one point on page 68, which, in my view, is not accurate, referring to 4-, 4.500, and then the witness did not say yes. He said: "That's what I said. It varied." Now that is a very ambiguous answer. So to put now to the witness that he committed himself to 4- to 4.500 would be not admissible. If you -- and I think the witness is pretty -- after this answer, after line 11, what I see on my screen, I think you continued about, I think, background, et cetera, and is not about the numbers anymore. In view of our earlier ruling that it was misleading the witness then, it was misleading to put to the witness something not exactly what he said in the state court, to continue now with the Karadzic case where the same happened would be just as inadmissible as it was already in the Karadzic -- was already earlier here today in this courtroom. And -- in my view -- but perhaps no one was aware that in Karadzic it was inadmissible as well. In my view, but of course I'm not one of the Judges in that case, but I see that you are doing exactly the same what we considered not inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, my intention was just to explain to the witness after seeing the whole passage that we had just looked at his earlier testimony and that I had misconstrued his earlier testimony, to see what parts of this he would agree to. I had absolutely no intention to go further than to clarify the picture with the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be clear where as far as the Chamber is concerned the boundaries are. We'll ask the witness to put on his earphones again, and perhaps it's better not to refer to two instances of, in my view, inappropriate questioning -- inadmissible questioning when you want to elicit further evidence from the witness. If you could keep that in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- of course, Your Honours. Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in fairness I would like to explain to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to be completely fair, Mr. Radinkovic, it looks like I have misconstrued your answer in your previous testimony in the Sarajevo court, and please tell me if I now can put to you your position accurately. Your testimony in the Sarajevo court in the Kondic case was to the effect that 4- to 4.500 people in total in your estimate came through Manjaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Exactly. May I add something? May I? That was just my estimate. That is to say, I did not have a list that at a given moment or on a given date there were such and such a number of people. As security organ, that was my assessment. That at one moment, it could not have been more than 3.000 or 3.200, but no way could there have been 4.000 or 4.500. Physically they couldn't fit in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd note that it's break time. It seems like a good moment in other senses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a good moment to take a break. We take a break of 20 minutes and we'd like to see you back after the break. You may now follow the usher. We resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Stojanovic, the statement of the witness was redacted and that has been uploaded already early February. The same is true for the table of concordance. But copies of the redacted statement or copies of the new statement have -- new table of concordance have never been sent to Chambers' staff, and that creates all kind of confusion and misunderstandings. So therefore if you have -- we, as Judges, we look at the 92 ter statement and attachments to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if there is anything, any further new versions of it, Chamber staff should be provided with a copy of those newest versions so that they can be passed on to us and that we know exactly what is redacted. We had no idea before we came to court. Ms. Edgerton, if you're ready you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go on to another area now, Mr. Radinkovic, I just want to ask you a little bit about some of the information you found -- you and your team found on conducting your interrogations. Now, it's correct, isn't it, that your team, as you processed the prisoners who came into Manjaca, found that a substantial number -- a larger number of the detainees hadn't been involved in the armed conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you found that a larger number hadn't been arrested with any weapons. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that was available to us, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your team actually reported this to the 1 KK command, didn't they? You told them that there was no basis for these people, who we've just referred to, to be kept prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But after our interviews and after having learned things directly from them or from other persons who were there. It is only then that we could provide information to the service or, rather, submit our own impressions, or perhaps a better word would be "notes," "observations," namely, that among them there were people who could go for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that included people who were elderly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: It particularly included the old and frail and a few persons who were underage who were there. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: People who were sick?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: The sick certainly. Especially those who were seriously ill. Usually they were both old and ill, so then we insisted and asked that primarily they be taken for a medical examination at the clinical centre, and some people were actually taken directly from the clinical centre to Geneva and elsewhere for medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to tie up again another couple of things that you mention in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I intervene for one --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you just explained to us, you said, and that was the start -- the question was that among them there would be people who could go for an exchange, and you then went through various categories, the old, the frail, the sick, the youngsters. My question is: Why didn't you release them? Why would they have to be exchanged? I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't have the right to release anyone or to detain anyone. We got the people that we got, and after our processing we could make proposals or propose certain measures to our superiors in terms of what should be done further. It is only after that. We couldn't just do anything off the cuff. And we could not release them. No chance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand from what I read here that they were no real prisoners of war. They had never been engaged in combat, there were the old ones, the youngsters, the sick ones. To say -- do you have any idea why your superiors, who had to decide why they could keep them at all, why were they in detention? Why were they there to be exchanged rather than to be immediately released, there being no proper basis for detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our superiors did not even bring them in; that is to say that they were arrested or brought in by the civilian police or, rather, even the military in various territories. For those reasons that they knew. For some we received documentation that they had taken part in armed conflict or in arming or in any other kind of organisation. So -- I mean, they were all brought together. It was not written anywhere this person is a soldier, that person is just a participant or an accomplice in different -- I mean, well, revealing our positions or whatever else. They were all brought there, all of those who were suspects. And it is only then that we would learn who could be qualified for certain things, held accountable for what they had possibly done, and then we made proposals that others be exchanged. That was our proposal and usually we were the ones initiating the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Why didn't you propose them to be released immediately because you found that there was no reason for detention, and apparently you accepted that a certain percentage of those brought in were detained without any proper legal basis. Why didn't you propose them to be released, let them go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, as professional security organs, could have done that too. But again, you have to bear in mind that it is 1992. War. And how can you release them when after 5 or 10 metres they would be liquidated by one side or the other. There is no way that they could have been released. They just had to be taken away somewhere to -- in an organised fashion. But our mandate was only to make proposals for an exchange, organised release, not just any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I understand you well that you exchanged them in order to protect them against violence by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only from violence, if you mean the camp. We protected them from the combat 20 kilometres away from Banja Luka. If they were to go in that direction, they would be in danger. Their lives would be in danger. There was a war going on. You cannot just go whichever way you wanted. That was our motto and that is what guided us. And I think that was humane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Serbs continued to live in those war areas as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Serbs and loyal Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you have people in detention where you have found out that they are not in any way involved in combat or there is no reason to detain them. Why not send them back to where the other loyal Muslims and the Serbs were living and allowing them to go home to their own houses but instead exchange them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, our proposal was aimed at them leaving the camp of Manjaca. Now, was that an exchange or perhaps a return to their place of residence and so on and so forth, I mean, well, that was for the other organs. It was for the command or civilian structures. Our notes were sent through our department and command to the security services centre, too. So perhaps they assessed that it was undesirable for them to come there for security reasons or whatever it was. But we did not receive any return information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, a minute ago you told me that -- you told this Chamber that you proposed them for exchange because it would otherwise be too dangerous. And now two minutes later, you say your proposal was aimed at them leaving Manjaca, exchange or return to their place of residence was the same. That -- those two answers are not consistent. Do you have any explanation for why you started with saying that you proposed an exchange and that two minutes later you say, well, it was not to be exchanged but it was just that they could leave Manjaca? Any explanation for this inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. If I put it vice versa, it would be clear. If we had made a proposal and not received an answer, then the next step would be to propose an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go to another area to end off our day, Mr. Radinkovic, this morning you spoke about a large group of prisoners who were brought in from a collection centre who were in a really bad state.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was at temporary transcript page 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, that's the same group as the 1.460 prisoners from Omarska that you referred to in your statement at paragraph 42; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's the group. And it was characteristic because just a month or two before, images from that camp, Omarska or Keraterm or whatever it was, were published all around the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to fill in the story about those prisoners. You said at -- in your statement, actually, at page 11, paragraph 12, you talked about them being locked inside buses overnight. So let's be perfectly clear: That huge group was actually brought to Manjaca on the 6th of August; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the document here, but I suppose that's correct. I mean, I can't remember off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they came in a large number of buses, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, 1.430 of them were packed into only 11 buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where they were made to spend the night was about 50 metres outside the barbed wire perimeter; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't spend the night there. They arrived around 3.00 or 4.00 a.m., so it was almost dawn. They were brought there and they were not forced but I can't remember for what reason they were supposed to hand in documents according to our procedure, and they were not able to do that. They had expected that we would just open the gate and receive them all at once. We, of course, refused and that caused the delay in admission, and of course we wanted to do it by day, in daylight.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these prisoners you found when processing them came with no papers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were without papers. Some of them had IDs or driver's licences or something, but perhaps 70 per cent of them were without any documents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you seek clarification of the words used by the witness, page 75, line 6: "They were brought there and they were not forced but I can't remember ..." Not forced to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, the transcript records you as saying, in respect of these prisoners we're talking about: "They were brought there and they were not forced but I can't remember for what reason they were supposed to hand in documents according to our procedure." Now perhaps we missed something in the interpretation or the transcription but perhaps -- maybe you're in a position to clarify that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was trying to say, since they had no proper documentation, and proper documentation would have been a whole complete list, bus by bus, with names and all the other details. They didn't have that. They didn't have the documents they were supposed to hand over to us. So I stopped them. I wanted to wait for sunrise and for them to make the lists properly, and to conduct the hand-over process as appropriate. That's what caused the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then who had to make those lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lists should have been made by those who had sent them to Manjaca camp. That means the civilian service in Prijedor that was in charge of the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I still do not know what these persons were not forced into. I still do not understand where you said, "... they were not forced ..." They were forced to stay in the buses, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were not allowed to leave the bus. Their escorts were made to produce the documents we required, the lists and all the rest. Not the prisoners but the escorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time you said it would be better to wait and leave up to 130 persons in a bus for hours and hours. You thought that, I think you said it was -- you earlier used the word "humane." Did you consider this appropriate to those in those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, we didn't know anything. We didn't know even the total number or the number of people per bus, we as a service didn't know that. We found out only when they began to disembark from the buses how many of them there were. Before that, we didn't have the elements to decide that we should start something earlier or start with interviews, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at a distance of 50 metres from the camp, you're unable to see that those buses were packed with 130 people in one bus, where a bus ordinarily takes, if I'm not wrong, 50 or 60 people. So that is more than double the number of passengers you would normally have on a bus. You couldn't see that from 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regrettably, my office is 150 metres away and I was not in a position to go out and interrogate the military police because it's the military police that was in charge of the external security of the camp. All this was happening away from me. They were just standing there. The buses were just standing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Edgerton, I need two or three minutes to continue to read a decision with which I started, so therefore if you could conclude in one or two minutes. I don't know whether you have any -- whether it's possible to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just try one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, once your service was able to process these prisoners who had been brought from Omarska, you realised that quite a number of them actually didn't deserve to be treated as prisoners of war either, didn't you? They didn't have weapons, they hadn't participated in combat. They didn't deserve to be there, did they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, later we realised that once we started to process this them. We worked continuously on a fast-track because we had received very little description of their prior activities and we had to work very quickly to establish the facts; in other words, to find out whether they were responsible for anything or we should propose some way for them to leave the camp. Just as the people who had been brought from other collection centres, from Kljuc, from Sanski Most, we processed them again. In fact, our service was doing its job regardless of the accompanying documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that takes us to the time-limit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radinkovic, we'll adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, but I would first instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way, irrespective of whom it is, about your testimony, testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I resume reading the half-read decision on the admission of documents used and tendered through the testimony of Vladimir Lukic. I left off after I had admitted -- well, the Chamber had admitted P6733 into evidence. P6734, P6740, and P6742 were marked for identification pending an agreement between the parties as to which portions should be tendered. The Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber through an e-mail on the 18th of December, 2014, that it seeks to have P6734 - that is, six pages - admitted in full and has provided excerpts of P6740 and P6742. The excerpts have Rule 65 ter numbers 7593a, which is six pages, and 2395a, which is 14 pages, respectively. The Defence has been asked to provide its position on these documents but has declined to do so. E-mails were sent on the 8th of January, the 8th of February, and again on the 13th of February, all of this year. The Chamber therefore understands that it does not object. The Chamber hereby admits P6734 into evidence. Further, the Chamber admits 65 ter 7593a and 2395a as P6740 and P6742, respectively. Six documents tendered by the Defence were also marked for identification pending an agreement between the parties as to which portions of the lengthy documents should be tendered. These are D629, D630, D633, D634, D635, and D639. The Chamber was informed via an e-mail on the 25th of November and the 11th of December, 2014, that an agreement had been reached between the parties and that the relevant excerpts had been uploaded under different Rule 65 ter numbers. The Chamber admits Rule 65 ter 1D5285 as D629, 1D5283 as D630, 1D2461 as D633, 1D5282 as D634, 1D5290 as D635, and 1D5281 as D639. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The Chamber will decide on the admission of associated exhibits for Witness Lukic in a separate decision. We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 17th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
